items.title: What happens if you do not brush your teeth for a year
items.text: If you stop oral hygiene , the balance between helpful bacteria and harmful pathobionts in your mouth quickly breaks down. Within just a few days, harmful bacteria multiply and create a sticky layer called dental plaque. This plaque irritates your gums, which can cause bleeding and inflammation , an early stage of disease called gingivitis. Within a month, the bacteria produce strong acids that eat away at tooth enamel and create painful cavities. If left untreated for several months, gingivitis worsens into periodontitis, which damages soft gum tissue and causes gums to pull away from your teeth. After a year without cleaning, chronic infection destroys the underlying bone and causes teeth to wobble and fall out. Even worse, damaged gums allow harmful bacteria to enter your bloodstream. From there, these microbes can travel through the body and worsen serious health conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and memory disorders like Alzheimer’s. Difficult words: oral hygiene (keeping your mouth clean and free of disease by regular brushing and flossing), pathobiont (a potentially disease-causing microorganism that normally lives harmlessly in the body unless the balance is disrupted), inflammation (when part of the body becomes red, swollen, hot, and often painful as a reaction to injury or infection), enamel (the hard, shiny outer surface layer of a tooth). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: What happens if you do not brush your teeth for a year
items.text: Your mouth needs daily cleaning to stay healthy. If you stop brushing and flossing , bad bacteria grow very fast. In just a few days, sticky plaque covers your teeth, and your gums bleed and swell. This early stage is called gingivitis. After a month, the bacteria break down tooth enamel and form cavities . If you ignore your teeth for a year, the infection gets much worse. Your gums pull away, the bone holding your teeth shrinks, and your teeth can fall out. Even worse, bad bacteria can get into your blood and cause serious health problems in your heart, kidneys, and brain. Brushing twice a day stops these dangerous bugs and protects your whole body. Difficult words: floss (to use a soft thread to clean between the teeth), plaque (a sticky film of bacteria on teeth), enamel (the top layer of a tooth), cavity (a hole in a tooth). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: What happens if you do not brush your teeth for a year
items.text: Brushing your teeth every day keeps your mouth healthy. If you stop cleaning your mouth, bad bacteria grow very fast. In a few days, your gums start to bleed and hurt. After a month, the bugs make holes in your teeth. We call these holes cavities. If you go a full year without brushing, your teeth can fall out. Also, the bacteria can get into your blood and make your heart, brain, and body sick. Brushing two times a day keeps your mouth clean, saves your teeth, and helps your body stay strong and happy. Difficult words: bacteria (small living organisms), gum (the pink flesh from where teeth grow), bleed (to lose blood, the red liquid in your body). items.title: Computers in Singapore hospitals stop working
items.text: A nine-and-a-half-hour IT outage that disrupted Singapore’s public healthcare clusters on October 13 was caused by a preventable error by an IT contractor. Senior Minister of State for Health told Parliament that the service provider failed to complete a required security update to the system. The disruption affected appointment bookings, medication dispensing , and billing across three major healthcare clusters. About 4,000 outpatient appointments had to be rescheduled. Although backup data centers were in place, both relied on the same shared system, which prevented an immediate recovery. Health officials confirmed that the incident was not a cyberattack and no patient data was compromised or lost. Healthcare workers successfully switched to manual procedures and ensured no patient safety incidents occurred. Difficult words: preventable (able to be stopped, avoided, or prevented before it happens), dispense (to prepare and give out medicine, goods, or services to people), compromised (weakened, damaged, or made vulnerable to security risks or failure). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Computers in Singapore hospitals stop working
items.text: On October 13, Singapore’s public hospitals faced a nine-and-a-half-hour computer system failure . It happened because a tech company hired to update security rules didn’t do the work on time. The outage affected major services, including booking appointments, giving out medicine, and paying bills. About 4,000 patient visits had to be moved to other days, but no patients were hurt. Health leaders said the problem was not a cyberattack, and no private medical data was stolen. Doctors and nurses quickly used paper rules and manual backups to keep taking care of patients. The health agency is now checking the contractor’s work and fixing the system so that future technical mistakes don’t cause problems again. Difficult words: failure (a situation in which a system stops working correctly), outage (a period of time when a service, power supply, or computer system is not working), private (belonging to a specific person or group, not public). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Computers in Singapore hospitals stop working
items.text: Hospital computers in Singapore stop working for almost ten hours on October 13. An IT company makes a mistake. They do not update the safety software on time. This makes it hard for people to get medicine, pay bills , or book visits. About 4,000 people must change their doctor visits to another day. But officials say that nobody is hurt and personal data is safe too. Doctors and nurses work by hand on paper to keep helping sick people. Leaders say sorry for the mistake. They are fixing the computers so this does not happen again. Difficult words: update (to make something more modern or install new software), bill (a document which shows how much money you must pay), fix (to repair something). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Chef fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizza
items.text: An Italian chef in Brisbane, Australia, has been fired for refusing to put pineapple on pizzas, among other reasons. He went to the Fair Work Commission to fight his dismissal, but failed to get his job back. The chef stated that topping pizzas with the tropical fruit was an "insult to his culture". He claimed he was sacked from a restaurant in May after repeatedly refusing his boss's instructions to make pineapple and ham pizzas for diners. His employer contended that the refusal was one of several workplace issues. The commission rejected the chef's application because it was submitted after the deadline. The chef has since found a job at another Italian restaurant. The question of whether pineapple belongs on pizza is a controversial one. It continues to divide public opinion. Pizza purists are aghast at the idea, but it is an established menu staple in many countries. The Hawaiian pizza was reportedly invented in Canada in 1962 after a chef used ham and pineapple as toppings. The restaurant owner expressed his opinion on it. He admitted that while the pizza was not his "absolute favourite," he would not "turn his nose up at it". Many restaurateurs insist that customers should be free to enjoy whatever ingredients and toppings they choose. items.title: Man completes 28-year walk around the world
items.text: A British man has completed an amazing 28-year walk around the world. Former soldier Karl Bushby, 57, arrived home in the city of Hull in England on Monday. He started his adventure in November 1998 in Chile, South America. His plan was to walk all the way home without using cars, boats, buses, trains, or airplanes. During his journey, he travelled about 58,000 kilometres through 29 countries. He crossed frozen seas, deserts, mountains, and jungles. He also faced many dangers. These included encountering polar bears and kidnappers, and spending time in a Russian prison. His journey was expected to take 12 years. However, problems with money, visas, and borders made his trip a lot longer. Thousands of people welcomed Mr Bushby home. He was very happy to finally finish his journey. His mother was waiting outside his childhood home to greet him. Bushby joked: "Sorry to keep you waiting." He also told the cheering crowd that many people around the world had helped him get home. He said he could not have done it alone. Britain's Prime Minister congratulated him on his achievement. He praised Bushby's determination and belief in himself. Bushby told the Guardian newspaper that he wasn't so interested in walking. He said: "It's boring as hell." That didn't stop him walking across four continents. items.title: Study finds majority of pilots nod off mid-flight
items.text: A new report has raised serious concerns about pilot fatigue. The European Cockpit Association (ECA) conducted a survey of nearly 7,200 pilots across 32 countries. It discovered that exhaustion in the cockpit is a widespread and underreported problem. More than three-quarters of respondents said they had briefly dozed off while operating an aircraft in the month before the survey. Almost a quarter of them admitted they continued flying even when they were too tired. Furthermore, half said they had operated a flight when they should have declared themselves unfit for duty. Tiredness can result from long working hours, insufficient rest, and unpredictable schedules. The pilots were very frank in their answers to the survey questions. Many said they were reluctant to report fatigue because they feared punishment or other negative reactions from their bosses. Captain Coen George, a director of the ECA, warned: "When pilots fear career consequences, fatigue goes unreported and the risk returns to the cockpit." Aviation safety experts say exhaustion can impair judgement, slow reaction times and prevent pilots from responding effectively to unexpected in-flight situations. The experts urged airlines to foster a culture in which pilots can report tiredness without fear of repercussions. Carriers should ensure that passenger safety is their top priority. items.title: World-famous London shopping street pedestrianized
items.text: One of London's most famous shopping streets has been pedestrianized. This means no cars, buses, trucks, or motorbikes can enter it. The street is called Oxford Street. It is well known all over the world. It used to be full of traffic. The Mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, decided to make it pedestrian-only. Around one kilometre of the street is off limits to vehicles. However, delivery trucks can use the area between midnight and 7 am. Mayor Khan hopes the pedestrianization will bring more shoppers back to the area. He called it a very important event for London. Mr Khan also plans to plant more trees along the street, create public squares, and add more seats and tables. There have been mixed reactions to the pedestrianization of Oxford Street. Many people support the plan. They are happy that the area will be less polluted. Khan said a traffic-free Oxford Street would "unlock the full potential" of an important area of London and help make a better, greener, and richer London. Around half a million people visit the street every day. However, many Londoners are unhappy that the street has been closed to traffic. Local official Tim Barnes said: "Traffic will be pushed to the small streets nearby causing economic and environmental harm." The Spectator magazine warned that life for car drivers would be harder. items.title: Parents take children out of big schools
items.text: More Danish parents are pulling their children out of mainstream schools. They argue that the traditional education system is far too rigid for neurodivergent kids. Children with autism or attention disorders, like 12-year-old Olav, often struggle with noisy classrooms and fixed daily schedules. Because public schools lack resources and specialized programs, many families have turned to alternative support systems, such as parent-led clubs. These spaces allow children to learn at their own pace through practical activities, like organic farming, while giving them a safe environment free from pressure. While politicians worry about falling academic standards in reading and math, educational researchers argue that the school system itself needs urgent reform rather than forcing children to fit into outdated models. These alternative clubs aim to rebuild confidence and help kids rebuild their relationship with learning. Difficult words: rigid (unable to be changed or adapted; strictly set), neurodivergent (having a brain that processes information differently than what is considered typical), academic standards (the levels of quality, knowledge, and achievement expected from students in school). You can watch the video news lower on this page.

items.title: Parents take children out of big schools
items.text: In Denmark, more and more parents are keeping their children home from traditional schools. Many neurodivergent children, like 12-year-old Olav, who has autism, find normal classrooms too loud and stressful. Because schools lack special resources, parents are creating alternative clubs. In these clubs, kids can learn outside by doing practical things, like working on organic farms or building boats, without feeling stressed. While government officials worry about test scores in reading and math, experts say the school system is old and needs big changes. Parents hope these new groups will give their kids a safe space to grow, feel happy again, and slowly return to learning. Difficult words: neurodivergent (thinking, learning, or behaving differently from most other people), lack (to not have enough of something, or to be completely without it), test score (a number or mark that shows how well a student did on an exam). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Parents take children out of big schools
items.text: Many parents in Denmark are taking their kids out of big schools. Normal classrooms are too loud and hard for some children. A boy named Olav has autism . He only goes to school a few hours a week. He mostly learns outside on a farm with his family. Parents are starting local groups where kids can play, work with their hands, and feel safe without stress. Experts say that schools need to change because kids learn in different ways today. These groups help families stay happy and keep learning every day. Difficult words: loud (not quiet), autism (a change in a person’s brain which impacts thinking, speaking, and understanding the world), local (when something is in an area or neighborhood near you). You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Mummy removed from exhibition over 'lack of consent'
items.text: A museum in Scotland has removed the remains of an ancient Egyptian mummy from an exhibition because there is no documented evidence that the deceased gave consent for their remains to be displayed. Glasgow's Kelvingrove Art Gallery and Museum took away the remains of a priest named Nakht, a mummified male head, and other body parts. In place of the exhibits, visitors found signs explaining that the remains had been removed "as a mark of respect". The museum said the decision "reflects contemporary museum practice". It added: "In the absence of consent, we believe removing ancient Egyptian human remains from display is more respectful to the deceased individuals." The decision has provoked widespread criticism. Scottish politician Murdo Fraser called the move "woke madness". He argued that museums should showcase history rather than hide it. A museum visitor complained that his daughter was upset at not being able to see the exhibits. An education campaigner said the decision "represents the triumph of educational stupidity and ignorance". He added: "It is not possible to seek permission from those who died thousands of years ago." However, the museum defended its action. It cited the International Council of Museums' Code of Ethics, which says museums "should uphold the inherent dignity of human remains". Buy my 1,000 Ideas and Activities for Language Teachers eBook. items.title: Hackers attack Ukrainian and Russian emergency apps
items.text: Both Ukraine and Russia recently reported that their official emergency alert apps were hit by major cyberattacks, which triggered mass panic through fake notifications. In Kyiv, citizens received terrifying false warnings about nuclear radiation, chemical threats, and active street fighting, and they were told to stay inside. Ukrainian officials quickly blamed Russian hackers and reassured the public that the actual air defense systems were never compromised . Just hours later, Russia’s Ministry of Emergency Situations reported a similar cyberattack on its own app, which sent out fake alerts with Ukrainian phrasing and offensive language. These attacks target popular mobile apps that millions rely on daily as a backup to air raid sirens . Experts point out that both countries have advanced hacking teams, and digital sabotage is a key weapon for wearing down morale , creating chaos, and making ordinary people doubt official safety warnings on both sides of the war. Difficult words: compromised (weakened, damaged, or made vulnerable to unauthorized access or security failure), air raid siren (a loud device used to warn the public of an incoming air attack or missile threat), sabotage (destroying or damaging something on purpose to stop it from working), morale (the confidence, enthusiasm, and discipline of a person or group at a particular time).
